# How to write a polite but firm complaint email that actually gets a reply

> **In short:** You can ask any AI assistant — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, or another — to draft a complaint email that stays calm, lists the facts, and ends with one clear ask. The trick is giving it the right facts and tone instructions; it can write the draft in seconds, but you still need to read it aloud, cut it to one ask, and send it yourself.

You've had a bad experience with a company. Maybe a product arrived broken, a bill is wrong, or support stopped replying. You want to complain, but you don't want to sound rude — and you really want a reply this time. An AI assistant can help you write a message that's hard to ignore: short, factual, polite, and impossible to misread. Here's how to do it in about 15 minutes.

## Before you start
- **An AI assistant you can type into.** Any major one works (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, DeepSeek). A free account is enough for this task.
- **A real complaint in mind.** Pick one you actually need to send — vague practice complaints don't teach you much.
- **About 15 minutes.** Most of that time is reading the draft out loud and editing, not waiting for the AI.

One honest note before we start: the assistant can draft the email, but it can't send it for you, and it can't guarantee a reply. What it *can* do is remove the hardest part — finding the right words when you're frustrated.

## Step 1 — Write down the five facts a rep will need

Before you open any AI tool, get the facts out of your head and onto paper (or a notes app). The biggest reason complaint emails get ignored is that they're vague. A sentence like "Your service is terrible" gives a customer-service rep nothing to act on.

Open a blank note and answer five questions in one or two short sentences each: (1) What did you buy or sign up for, and when? (2) What went wrong? (3) What have you already tried to fix it? (4) What do you want them to do now? (5) What's your deadline for a response?

💬 Example: "Bought a blue wool coat from Example Outfitters on March 4 (order #1234). It arrived March 10 with a torn lining. Emailed support on March 11, no reply. I'd like a replacement shipped by March 25, or a full refund."

You'll know it worked when you can read the note out loud in under 30 seconds and someone else would understand what happened without asking follow-up questions.

## Step 2 — Open your AI assistant and start a fresh chat

Open the AI assistant you normally use, on whatever device is handy — phone, tablet, or computer. When the chat window opens, start a new conversation rather than continuing an old one. A fresh chat gives the assistant a clean slate, so it won't accidentally mix in tone or facts from a previous topic.

Look for a button like a **"New chat"**, **"+"**, or **pencil icon** near the top or side of the screen. On some apps it lives inside a menu (often three dots or three lines). If you can't find it, just refresh the page or close and reopen the app — most assistants start you on a blank conversation by default.

💬 Example: type "I want to draft a complaint email" as your first line, just to confirm the chat is responding.

You'll know it worked when you see a blank message box at the bottom of the screen and the assistant is ready for your prompt.

## Step 3 — Paste a prompt that names the facts, the tone, and the ask

Now copy the five facts from Step 1 and paste them into the chat, followed by a short set of instructions. The clearer your instructions, the closer the first draft will be to something you'd actually send.

Type something like the prompt below — adjust the wording to your situation, but keep the same four pieces: facts, tone, length, and ask.

💬 Example: "Please draft a polite but firm complaint email. Facts: [paste your five facts here]. Tone: calm, professional, no sarcasm, no insults. Length: under 150 words. End with one specific ask and a reasonable deadline of 5 business days. Do not invent any order numbers, dates, or names I didn't give you."

You'll know it worked when the assistant produces a complete email — greeting, facts, what you want, deadline — in one block of text that reads like a real human wrote it. If the first draft comes out too long, too stiff, or too emotional, that's normal; you'll fix that in the next step.

## Step 4 — Read the draft out loud and tame the tone

Don't send the first draft yet. Read it out loud, slowly. Your ear catches things your eyes miss — awkward phrases, sentences that sound angrier than you feel, or phrases that sound so polite they sound sarcastic.

If a sentence makes you wince, copy that one sentence back into the chat and ask the assistant to rewrite it in a calmer voice. Don't throw the whole draft away; most of it is probably fine. Common rewrites you'll want: "I'm extremely disappointed" becomes "I'd like this resolved"; "This is unacceptable" becomes "I'd like to understand what happened"; "You need to fix this immediately" becomes "I'd appreciate a response by [date]."

If the draft came out too apologetic — sounding like you're asking permission to complain — say so directly. 💬 Example: "Make this sound more confident. I'm being reasonable, but I expect a real answer."

You'll know it worked when you can read the email aloud without rolling your eyes, and a friend would describe the tone as "firm but polite" — not angry, not groveling.

## Step 5 — Cut the email down to one clear ask

A complaint email that asks for three different things often gets three different "we'll look into it" replies and nothing actually happens. Read the draft and circle the single most important thing you want.

If the email mentions a refund, a replacement, an apology, and a discount, pick the one that matters most and cut the others. You can always bring up the others in a later email if the first ask is refused. Then paste the draft back into the chat and ask for the trim.

💬 Example: "Shorten this to one ask: I want a replacement coat shipped by March 25. Remove the part about the discount."

You'll know it worked when the last paragraph of the email contains exactly one sentence that begins with "I'd like" or "Please" and ends with a specific date. Everything else in the email is supporting context, not a wish list.

## Step 6 — Send it, save the thread, and set a follow-up reminder

Copy the final draft into your real email app, fill in the real order number, your name, and any attachments (photos of the damage, receipts, screenshots of the original chat). Read it one last time to make sure no detail was lost in the copy-paste — small errors like a wrong date can undo an otherwise strong email.

Before you hit send, take a screenshot of the email and save the AI chat somewhere you can find it. If you have to follow up later, you'll have a record of exactly what you asked for. Then set a calendar reminder for two business days after your stated deadline.

💬 Example follow-up: "Following up on my email below — I haven't received a response. I'd still like a replacement coat shipped by March 25. Please let me know either way."

You'll know it worked when the email is sitting in your sent folder, you have a date on your calendar for the follow-up, and you feel — for the first time in this whole mess — that you've said exactly what you needed to say.

## Common mistakes

- **Letting the AI invent facts.** If you say "I ordered something last month," the assistant may invent an order number or date that sounds real but isn't. Always paste your *own* facts, and add the line "Do not invent any details I didn't give you."
- **Sending the first draft without reading it.** AI drafts are usually 80% right and 20% wrong in tone. The 20% is what makes an email sound robotic or slightly off. Always read it out loud.
- **Asking for too many things at once.** "I want a refund, a replacement, an apology, and a discount" usually gets you nothing. Pick one ask, and bring up the others later if needed.
- **Copying a tone that doesn't sound like you.** If the draft sounds too stiff or too formal, paste in a sentence you've actually written before — a text to a friend, an older email — and ask the assistant to match that voice.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** The next time a delivery is wrong, a bill is off, or a service lets you down, you'll have a way to complain that takes 15 minutes instead of an evening of staring at a blank screen.
- **For your business or work:** The same method works for vendor disputes, late invoices, or client complaints. A calm, one-ask email is also the right tone when you're escalating an issue to a manager — you sound professional, not emotional.
- **If you're just getting started:** The very first email to draft this way is the hardest. After that, you'll have a prompt template you can reuse with new facts pasted in.

## Try it now

Open your AI assistant, paste this prompt, and fill in the five facts from Step 1: *"Draft a polite but firm complaint email. Facts: [your facts]. Tone: calm and professional. Length: under 150 words. End with one specific ask and a 5-business-day deadline. Do not invent any details."* Read the result out loud, trim it to one ask, and you'll have a sendable email in under 10 minutes.
